questions.question: Explain why official statistics may not provide an accurate picture of crime.

points.text: Official statistics underestimate crime because: most crime is not reported (dark figure); police do not record all reported crime. The CSEW suggests real crime is about twice the official figure. Self-report studies show middle-class crime is underrepresented.

questions.question: Evaluate explanations for why men commit more crime than women.

points.text: Men commit 80% of recorded crime. Heidensohn: patriarchal control restricts women's opportunities. Chesney-Lind: women's crime often responds to abuse. However: the gap is narrowing; female crime is rising; biological explanations (testosterone) are reductionist.

questions.question: Assess whether ethnic differences in crime statistics reflect real differences in criminality.

points.text: Black people are over-represented in official statistics but this reflects: selective policing (stop and search 9x higher for Black people), labelling, socio-economic factors. Self-report studies show similar offending across ethnic groups. Conclusion: ethnic differences reflect bias in the CJS, not higher criminality.

points.text: A grade 9 response will: describe official statistics and their strengths (comprehensive, regularly collected); explain limitations (dark figure, selective reporting, recording practices); compare with alternatives (self-report, victim surveys); evaluate bias; conclude: official statistics are useful for broad patterns but significantly distort the true picture. Triangulation using multiple sources provides a more accurate understanding.
